questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Introduce a new angle: runtime-extensible evaluation logic for feature flags to reflect real-world needs in large orgs.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy pattern for evaluators
- Registry for dynamic extension
- Composite rule composition (anyOf/allOf)
- EvalContext design and caching for performance

## Code Example
```typescript
interface Evaluator { evaluate(ctx: EvalContext): boolean }
type EvalContext = { user: any; time: Date; attrs: any }
class EvaluatorRegistry {
  register(name: string, factory: (cfg: any)=>Evaluator): void
  resolve(name: string, cfg: any): Evaluator
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How to model evaluation order and short-circuit semantics?
- How to handle cross-feature conflicts and auditing of evaluator registrations?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Beginner-friendly exploration of extensibility and non-blocking I/O: add new sinks without changing core, and isolate failures per sink.

## Key Concepts
- Strategy/Plug-in pattern for runtime extension
- Registry mapping names to Sink implementations
- Non-blocking writes via per-sink queuing and worker pool
- Fault isolation and graceful degradation

## Code Example
```typescript
interface Sink { write(msg: string): Promise<void> }
class Registry { addSink(name: string, s: Sink): void; getSinks(): Sink[] }
class Logger { constructor(private reg: Registry) ; log(msg: string): void { for (const s of reg.getSinks()) s.write(msg); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test sink isolation and backpressure?
- How would you implement graceful shutdown for all sinks?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a pluggable, runtime-extendable auth system with strong tenant isolation, security, and observability. Demonstrates plugin loading, DI patterns, and security considerations critical at scale.

## Key Concepts

- Plugin architecture with dynamic loading
- Tenant isolation and per-tenant configuration
- Authentication flows: login, refresh, logout
- Security: short‑lived tokens, revocation, audit trails

```typescript
interface LoginRequest { provider: string; tenantId: string; credentials: any }
interface AuthResult { token: string; expiresAt: number }

  login(req: LoginRequest): Promise<AuthResult>
  refresh(token: string): Promise<AuthResult>
  logout(token: string): Promise<void>
}
interface ProviderFactory {
  create(tenantId: string, config: any): AuthProvider
}
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you version and hot-swap providers without downtime?
- How would you test provider isolation and revocation at scale?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to extend behavior without touching core dispatch logic; demonstrates the Command pattern with a runtime registry.

## Key Concepts
- Command pattern
- Registry-based extensibility
- Safe, non-invasive extension

## Code Example
```javascript
interface Command { execute(args: string[]): void; }
class Registry { private map = new Map<string, Command>(); register(name: string, c: Command) { this.map.set(name, c); } get(name: string): Command | undefined { return this.map.get(name); } }
class Router { constructor(private registry: Registry) {} route(argv: string[]) { const cmd = argv[0]; const command = this.registry.get(cmd); if (command) command.execute(argv.slice(1)); else throw new Error('Unknown command'); } }
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle asynchronous commands? 
- How would you ensure thread-safety in a multi-process CLI?
